extracted.subtask_description: An undergraduate course project that uses Pascal's Treatise on the Arithmetical Triangle and Euler's Königsberg paper to teach mathematical induction, combinatorics (binomial coefficients), the binomial theorem and Fermat's Little Theorem, and Euler circuits; students must translate Pascal's prose into modern notation, prove stated consequences (often by induction), and complete exercises applying Euler's parity method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Ti;j index notation to identify nth-base numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use our index notation Ti;j to explain exactly which are the numbers in the n-th base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate Pascal's verbal descriptions of 'bases' into the project's Ti;j indexing; give explicit examples from Pascal's initial table to verify the mapping. (Exercise a)

rubrics_metrics.name: Write Seventh Consequence and proof in Ti;j notation
rubrics_metrics.description: In full generality, write the Seventh Consequence and its proof, using our Ti;j notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the consequence precisely in modern index notation and provide a rigorous proof (following Pascal's reasoning or modernizing it). (Exercise b)

rubrics_metrics.name: State and prove Eighth Consequence using induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the statement of the Eighth Consequence in our notation, using modern exponential notation to describe his double progression. Use summation notation as needed, and introduce additional new notation if helpful. Then prove the Eighth Consequence by mathematical induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express Pascal's 'double progression' succinctly (e.g., geometric progression), formalize the statement in Ti;j and summation/exponent notation, and produce a clear inductive proof. (Exercise c)

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelfth Consequence (ratio of contiguous cells)
rubrics_metrics.description: In every arithmetical triangle, of two contiguous cells in the same base the upper is to the lower as the number of cells from the upper to the top of the base is to the number of cells from the lower to the bottom of the base, inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite this Twelfth Consequence in modern generalized formula form (Ti;j) and verify with examples from Pascal's table. Then adapt Pascal's example proof into a general inductive proof. This is flagged as 'most important and famous' in the treatise. (Exercises 6a, 6b)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute cell value from perpendicular and parallel exponents (Pascal's Problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the perpendicular and parallel exponents of a cell, to find its number without making use of the arithmetical triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Pascal's product/quotient procedure (multiply sequences of integers starting at the parallel exponent, divide by product of preceding integers up to perpendicular exponent minus one). Show the algebraic reasoning using the Twelfth Consequence or factorial notation; note the N.B. about a non-unity generator. Work the provided example (5th perpendicular, 3rd parallel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express Pascal's general formula for Ti;j in factorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down the general formula Pascal claims in solving his 'Problem.' Your formula should read Ti;j 'some formula in terms of i and j.' Also write your formula entirely in terms of factorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the binomial-coefficient-style formula (Ti;j in terms of factorials) and give a general proof either following Pascal's indicated reasoning or by induction. (Exercise 7a, 7b)

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate triangle entries to combinations (Proposition 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of any cell is equal to the number of combinations of a number less by unity than its parallel exponent in a number less by unity than the exponent of its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite Pascal's Proposition 2 using Ti;j notation: fill in the sentence 'Ti;j is the number of combinations of ____ things from ____ things.' Explain and justify via Pascal's Lemma/Proposition structure or modern combinatorial arguments. (Exercise 1b)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove Pascal's Lemma 4 (combinatorial identity) and connect to recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the number of combinations of k in n is the sum of the combinations of k-1 in n-1 and the combinations of k in n-1; explain why Proposition 2 follows from Proposition 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and prove the identity C(n,k)=C(n-1,k-1)+C(n-1,k) in the general case, using combinatorial reasoning; link this to Pascal's recursion and his presentation of the triangle. (Optional/advanced part of 1c)

rubrics_metrics.name: Express binomial coefficients in Ti;j and factorial notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern symbol n choose r means the number of ways of choosing r things from amongst n things. Explain how this is related to what we have been learning about the Arithmetical Triangle from reading Pascal. In particular, explain how the numbers Ti;j are related to the numbers n choose r. Write Ti;j in n choose r notation and manipulate it to express it entirely in terms of factorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate between Ti;j and C(n,r) notation and derive the factorial expression C(n,r)=n!/(r!(n-r)!). Also discuss permutations vs combinations. (Exercise 2a, 2b)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counting-of-combinations proof of the binomial theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Read in a modern textbook about the binomial theorem. Write an explanation of the proof of the binomial theorem using the idea of counting combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a combinatorial derivation of the binomial expansion coefficients using combinations as counts of choices of terms in product expansions. (Part Three, 1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover and prove Fermat's Little Theorem via Pascal tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a table of remainders of a^n upon division by n for a,n up to 14, conjecture the form a^p ≡ a (mod p) (or a^{p} ≡ a (mod p) and related formulations), and write up a proof of Fermat’s Little Theorem by mathematical induction on a using the binomial theorem, Pascal's factorial formula, and uniqueness of prime factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect empirical data, state conjectures, then give a proof using the binomial theorem and divisibility analysis of binomial coefficients by a prime p. (Part Three, 2a–2c)

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional: Study and explain RSA cryptosystem
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and study the RSA cryptosystem and its applications to digital security, including how it works, which follows from Fermat’s Theorem. Write up the details in your own words, with some example calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional extension applying Fermat's theorem to public-key encryption; include worked numerical examples and explanation of key generation, encryption, decryption, and security reliance on prime factorization hardness. (Part Three, 3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn mathematical induction from Pascal's verbal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should learn the concept of mathematical induction and its application directly from reading Pascal's Treatise on the Arithmetical Triangle; Pascal offers a verbal condition for persistence of a pattern known today as mathematical induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read Pascal's Twelfth Consequence and associated arguments; then compare and formalize the induction principle in textbook axiomatic form. Instructor notes recommend using Pascal first, then supplementing with a modern textbook; the project may count as significant course percentage and be submitted incrementally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate the bridge problem as a graph (vertices/edges/walks/paths/circuits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the map by a diagram of points (land masses) and line segments (bridges); represent crossings by sequences of letters (vertices) and define walk, path, circuit; define connected graph and Euler path/circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the physical map into a graph abstraction, using vertex adjacency and edge incidence. Exercises ask to sketch graphs and to reason about required letters for an Euler path. Understand definitions so you can apply Euler's procedure. (Euler section, early paragraphs)

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's occurrence rule (parity-based letter counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define, corresponding to the number of bridges leading to each area, the number of occurrences of the letter denoting that area to be half the number of bridges plus one, if the number of bridges is odd, and if the number of bridges is even, to be half of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule to compute how many times each vertex must appear in a representation of a route that crosses every bridge once. Use these counts to test feasibility. (Euler paragraphs 8–12)

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's algorithmic test for existence of Euler path
rubrics_metrics.description: I first denote by the letters A, B, C, etc. the various areas ... I then take the total number of bridges, add one, and write the result above the working ... mark even-count vertices with an asterisk ... write half the even numbers and half the odd numbers plus one, add them; if this sum is equal to or one less than number_of_bridges+1 then a required journey is possible (starting point determined by parity); if greater, impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Euler's step-by-step worksheet method: list vertices with number of incident bridges, mark evens, compute half-values (or half+1 for odds), sum and compare to bridges+1. Use this to decide existence and starting area. (Euler paragraph 14 and worked examples)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Euler procedure and produce an explicit Euler path when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Euler-path test indicates existence, actually find and present a sequence of letters (or edges) representing a route that crosses each bridge exactly once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given an instance where the test indicates an Euler path/circuit, construct such a path explicitly (example provided in Euler paragraphs 15 and following). Students are asked to apply the procedure and, if positive, find one. (Exercise 5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate Euler's observations in degree-language and derive simplified condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate Euler's 'occurrence' and sum method into modern degree terminology (deg(v)) and restate the test as a condition on vertex degrees for existence of an Euler path/circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express his steps as: if a connected graph has all vertices of even degree there is an Euler circuit; if exactly two vertices have odd degree there is an Euler path starting and ending at odd-degree vertices; otherwise no Euler path exists. Derive this from Euler's counting argument and note simplifications. (Euler paragraphs 16–17 prompt this)

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically compare historical and modern proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on how convincing Euler's statements and arguments are (e.g., his claim 'the required journey can be found when the total of occurrences equals bridges+1') and how a modern textbook proof would differ in style and rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the difference in precision and methods between Euler's verbal/algorithmic argument and a modern graph-theoretic proof; discuss connectedness, parity arguments, and use of formal lemmas. (Euler paragraph 13 and Instructor notes)
